SMART Guidelines are Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable recommended digital capabilities, health and data content aligned with normative recommendations (17).
SMART Guidelines are WHO’s approach to systematize and accelerate the consistent application of recommended, life-saving interventions in the digital age.

The five knowledge layers comprise: • L1 Narrative: enhanced clinical, public health guidelines and data recommendations • L2 Operational: digital adaptation kits (DAKs) • L3 Machine readable: machine-readable recommendations Source: WHO SMART guidelines: optimising country-level use of guideline recommendations in the digital age (Mehl et al., 2021) (18). • L4 Executable: reference applications and services • L5 Dynamic: precision health model.

These layers inform developers how to translate recommendations into specifications and standards; technologists how to integrate recommendations into updatable digital systems; and countries how to localize, make interoperable, institutionalize and update digital systems consistent with evidence-based recommendations (17).

This chapter outlines the areas that should be analysed and the factors to consider.
The analysis should outline their roles in substandard and falsified medical products, pharmacovigilance and digital health.
It should help mobilize support and engage key players by examining responsibilities, information flows and power dynamics.
As one of the first steps, a digital readiness assessment should be conducted to ensure solutions are tailored to the existing infrastructure, capacity and context.

The outputs from the assessment should inform the necessary resources, enabling environment, budget and funding support for planning, implementation and operationalization of the substandard and falsified reporting system.
The following areas should be reviewed to assess the country's digital readiness. • National digital health strategy.
Are there any existing digital platforms or tools they use that must integrate with the substandard and falsified reporting system?
The presence of an existing digital health governance framework should also be assessed.
This assessment should determine network coverage across the entire country, including regional, rural and remote areas, while identifying any potential challenges. • Security and privacy protection.
The results of the assessment should inform planning necessary investments during implementation and operation stages.
The outputs of the analysis should be used to develop optimal business processes and workflows within the application.
As part of this analysis key pharmacovigilance structures, systems, procedures and mechanisms within the country should be identified.

After finishing the steps outlined in this chapter, there should be a comprehensive current state analysis of the key stakeholders including: Digital readiness Enabling environment Technology infrastructure Current reporting procedures Barriers to reporting End of chapter checklist

4.5 Gather requirements Functional and non-functional requirements outline what the reporting application needs to do and how it should perform.
Security – confidentiality Data at rest must be encrypted by the IT solution.
Industry best practice cryptographic algorithms must be enforced by the IT solution.
Security – confidentiality For sensitive data, secure data destruction processes must be in place.
There must be evidence of secure data destruction.
Security – confidentiality Data must be encrypted on all removable media used by the IT solution.
Security – confidentiality A solution should have all levels of technical support for security controls.
Security – authentication Multi-factor authentication must be enforced.
Security – authentication When authentication is required, all systems or applications should integrate with the single sign on authentication scheme (SAML; OpenID Connect) of the NMRA.
Security – audit trail and logs Audit history/trail/logs for all records should not be editable.

Security – general The hosting provider should produce evidence that security controls are in place (i.e. network and web application firewalls; proxy; etc.) including evidence of recent security audits and security penetration tests.

Security – general There must be a governance mechanism to ensure confidential and sensitive data (to be determined through a separate confidentiality undertaking) is sufficiently protected in accordance with the highest standards, and in compliance with all applicable laws, ordinances, rules and regulations (including the United Nations Principles on Personal Data Protection and Privacy).
System requirements – general Must have the ability to store images and other unstructured data.
System requirements – general The solution should be designed and certified according to ISO 27000 family.
System requirements – general All application software code must be created with exclusive intellectual property rights to NMRA.
System requirements – general The developer of software solution must ensure the legality of third-party software components usage.
System requirements – general System must support the transformation of report data into charts or graphs or any other standard visual representations.
System requirements – general System must support the creation and export of reports to MS Word, MS Excel, Email or PDF or any other universal standard.
System requirements – general System must support the import of data and reports in pdf, xls, rtf, txt, doc, csv formats.

As noted in WHO’s Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions: a practical guide to conducting research and assessment (8): “During the maturity life cycle of a digital health intervention, concurrent monitoring and evaluation (M&E) activities should be planned, often in parallel, supporting each other.
The framework should outline how the reporting application is expected to work and what outcomes it aims to achieve.
The design should be robust, ensuring that it can provide reliable and valid results that can inform decision-making.
Additionally, resources must be allocated to support these activities, including funding, personnel and data collection tools.
Step 6 All the above details must be summarized into an M&E implementation plan.
It should also include mechanisms for reviewing and updating the M&E plan to ensure it remains relevant and effective over time.
This plan should include details of stakeholders that will own and maintain the reporting application.
Recurring knowledge management needs, including training, updating job aids, recruitments and job rotations, must also be addressed in the plan.

Furthermore, the plan should outline the recurring costs for the required resources, system subscriptions, knowledge management, cybersecurity, M&E and efforts to maintain and operate the application.
This strategy should include budgeting for unexpected expenses and exploring potential funding sources.
A robust plan for data backups and system redundancy must be devised to mitigate the impact of system failures.
This process should include mechanisms for evaluating and prioritizing new requirements, as well as a structured approach to implementing changes.
After finishing the steps outlined in this chapter, the following outputs should be available: M&E plan Operations and sustainability plan End of chapter checklist 6.

User persona template A user persona template/worksheet that summarizes each and every type of end user (e.g. pharmacists, doctors, nurses, dentists, midwives, paramedics, laboratory technicians, public health workers, veterinarians and pharmacy technicians) should be completed.
Diagrams should be clear, neat and easy for all viewers to understand the relationships across the different swim lanes.
Start event or trigger event The workflow diagram should contain a start event and an end event, defining the beginning and completion of the task.
For clarity, there should be only one end event per swim lane.
Activity, process step or task Each activity should start with a verb, such as “register client” or “calculate risk”.
Between the start and end of a task, there should be a series of activities noting the successive actions performed by the actor for that swim lane.
If the diagram is too complex, the subprocess symbol should be used to reference another process depicted on another page.
The end event should not have any output arrows.
All symbols (except for the end event and gateway) should have one and only one output arrow, leading to a new symbol, looping back to a previously used symbol or to the end event symbol.
Connecting arrows should not cross over each other.
Only two different outputs should originate from a decision point.

If more than two output or sequence flow arrows are needed, you are likely trying to depict decision-support logic or a business rule, which should be depicted as an activity with a business rule instead (see above).
A catch – link event must follow the throw – link event.
A throw – link event must be aligned to a catch – link event.
The above selection of symbols should be sufficient, though, for the purposes of illustrating the business process workflows in a clear, standard way.

Notes: R (responsible) – person/organization that does the work; A (accountable) – decision-maker, approves the work; C (consulted) – provides input, must be consulted before the task is completed; I (informed) – needs updates on progress but not directly involved; UI – user interface; UX – user experience.
